source_data.subject: Social Science - Economics

details: Individual developmental aspirations vary based on socio-economic background, life situations, and immediate priorities.
Development for one individual or group may not be development for another, and can often be destructive for others.
evidence_or_examples: Industrialists desiring large dams for hydroelectricity vs. indigenous tribal communities facing displacement and loss of agrarian livelihoods.
Urban high-rise real estate expansion displacing local informal slum communities.

branches.theme: 1.2 Material Income & Non-Material Life Quality Goals

details: Besides regular and higher income, people seek non-material aspects of life essential for human dignity and well-being.
Key non-material goals include equal treatment, personal freedom, physical security, respect from others, non-discrimination, and safe working environment.
Women engaging in paid employment gain social dignity, which requires family acceptance, safety, and shared domestic responsibilities.
evidence_or_examples: Job offers considering distance, working atmosphere, and family security over mere monetary salary.
Female labor force participation improving household gender equality.

sub_branches.concept: Per Capita Income & World Bank Criteria
details: National development entails making fair, just, and inclusive choices benefiting the majority of citizens.
World Bank's World Development Reports compare nations using Per Capita Income (PCI = Total National Income / Total Population).
Thresholds (2021): High-income / Rich countries > USD 49,300 per annum; Low-income countries <= USD 2,500 per annum; India is Low-Middle Income (~USD 2,370/year).
evidence_or_examples: World Development Report classification table comparing high, middle, and low-income economies.
Country A vs. Country B comparison showing equal average income ($10,000) but extreme wealth concentration in Country B (one rich citizen earning $48,000 while four earn $500).

sub_branches.concept: UNDP Human Development Indicators vs. Income
details: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) publishes the Human Development Report, ranking countries on health, education, and GNI per capita.
State-level comparison in India: Haryana has higher Per Capita Income (₹2,36,147) than Kerala (₹2,21,904), but Kerala excels in health and education metrics.
Key Indicators: Infant Mortality Rate (Kerala 7 vs Haryana 30 per 1,000), Literacy Rate (Kerala 94% vs Haryana 80%), Net Attendance Ratio (Kerala 83% vs Haryana 61%).
Public Facilities: Collective provisions like Public Distribution System (PDS), public health centers, and state education cannot be replaced solely by individual private money.
evidence_or_examples: Tamil Nadu PDS reaching 90% rural population resulting in superior health/nutritional status compared to states with weak PDS.
Body Mass Index (BMI = Weight kg / [Height m]²) used as an adult health metric (<18.5 undernourished, >=25 overweight).

details: Sustainable development ensures present growth does not compromise the capabilities and natural assets of future generations.
Renewable resources (groundwater) replenish naturally, but over-exploitation leads to critical water table decline.
Non-renewable resources (crude oil, fossil fuels) have fixed global stocks and will be exhausted within decades at current consumption rates.
evidence_or_examples: Groundwater depletion in 1/3rd of Indian districts (over-pumping in agricultural regions of Punjab, Western UP, and hard-rock plateau areas of Central India).
Mahatma Gandhi's statement: 'The Earth has enough resources to meet the needs of all, but not enough to satisfy the greed of even one person.'

branches.theme: 2.1 Classification of Economic Activities (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary)

details: Primary Sector: Extraction and direct exploitation of natural resources (agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining, dairy).
Secondary Sector: Manufacturing and industrial processing transforming raw agricultural/mineral materials into finished goods (cotton to cloth, sugarcane to sugar, iron ore to steel).

Tertiary Sector: Support services that facilitate production and distribution in primary and secondary sectors without directly producing physical goods (transport, storage, communication, banking, IT, trade).
Interdependence: Disruption in one sector cascades across all others (e.g., transport strikes prevent crop delivery, rising fertilizer costs increase industrial input expense).
evidence_or_examples: Cultivation of cotton (Primary) → Processing into yarn & fabric (Secondary) → Transport & retail sales in market (Tertiary).
Call centers, software development, and banking services driving modern service sector growth.

branches.theme: 2.2 GDP Measurement & Historical Sectoral Shifts in India

sub_branches.concept: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) & Production vs. Employment Discrepancy
details: GDP / Gross Value Added (GVA) represents the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a financial year.
Double Counting Rule: Only final goods are counted; intermediate goods (e.g. wheat/flour used in biscuits) are excluded as their value is already embedded in the final price.

Historical Shift: Developed nations transitioned labor sequentially from Primary to Secondary to Tertiary. In India, Tertiary GDP share surged past 50%, but labor shift out of Agriculture lagged severely.
Employment Discrepancy: Primary sector generates under 16% of GDP but employs >44% of the Indian labor force.
evidence_or_examples: Graph analysis comparing 1973-74 vs 2013-14 GDP composition showing explosive Tertiary sector rise.
Baker buying flour for ₹10/kg and sugar for ₹40/kg to sell biscuit packets for ₹60; counting only the ₹60 prevents double counting.

details: Disguised Unemployment (Underemployment): Situations where more people work on an agricultural plot or small shop than needed; individual marginal productivity is zero.
Creating Employment: Infrastructure investment (dams, rural roads, cold storage), expanding bank credit for pumpsets/inputs, promoting agro-processing industries.

Statutory Guarantee: MGNREGA 2005 (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) enforces the legal 'Right to Work', guaranteeing 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households, providing unemployment allowance if work is not provided within 15 days.
evidence_or_examples: Laxmi's 2-hectare unirrigated farm where 5 family members work full-year; removing 2 members to work in a local dam project leaves farm yield unchanged while boosting family cash income.
Viksit Bharat-G RAM G 2025 initiative enhancing rural infrastructure employment.

sub_branches.concept: Organised vs. Unorganised & Public vs. Private Sectors
details: Organised Sector: Registered with government, follows statutory rules (Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act), offers job security, fixed hours, paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits, and pensions.
Unorganised Sector: Small, scattered unregistered units, outside regulatory control, characterized by low wages, no job security, no paid holidays, informal hiring/firing.
Public Sector: State-owned enterprises aimed at social welfare, providing essential infrastructure at subsidized rates (Indian Railways, Post Office).
Private Sector: Investor-owned enterprises driven by profit motives (TATA Motors, Reliance Industries).
evidence_or_examples: Kanta (Organised office employee receiving appointment letter, PF, paid Sunday) vs. Kamal (Unorganised grocery shop worker working 12 hours without paid leave or appointment letter).
Public sector constructing heavy capital projects (dams, bridges, power plants) that private investors avoid due to long payback periods.

branches.theme: 3.1 Money as a Medium of Exchange & Modern Currency

sub_branches.concept: Evolution from Barter to Demand Deposits
details: Barter System Friction: Relies on Double Coincidence of Wants (both parties holding exact complementary goods).
Money functions as an intermediate asset in transactions, eliminating double coincidence requirements.
Modern Currency: Paper notes and coins issued exclusively by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on behalf of the Central Government. Money is legally binding medium of payment.
Demand Deposits: Bank deposits withdrawable on demand via cash, cheques, debit cards, or UPI. A cheque instructs a bank to transfer funds directly between accounts without physical cash movement.
evidence_or_examples: Shoe manufacturer wanting wheat needing a farmer who wants shoes in a barter system vs. selling shoes for money and buying wheat freely.
Cheque transaction mechanism detailing Payee name, numeric amount, account payee crossing, 6-digit cheque number, and 9-digit MICR code.

details: Financial Intermediation: Banks hold ~15% of deposits as liquid cash reserve for daily withdrawals and lend out ~85% to borrowers.
Bank Income Spread: The margin between higher interest charged on loans and lower interest paid to depositors.
Virtuous Credit Cycle: Credit provides working capital, enhances production capacity, increases net earnings, and enables prompt loan repayment.
Vicious Credit Cycle (Debt Trap): Credit taken for crop production fails due to natural disasters/pests, leading to compounding high-interest debts that force asset/land sales.
evidence_or_examples: Salim (Shoe Manufacturer): Secures leather credit & bank advance for 3,000 shoe pairs festive order, completes delivery, earns profit, repays loan successfully.
Swapna (Small Farmer): Borrows from local moneylender for groundnut cultivation; crop fails due to pests despite spraying pesticides; forced to sell portion of land to clear debt.

branches.theme: 3.3 Terms of Credit & Formal vs. Informal Credit Sectors

sub_branches.concept: Terms of Credit, RBI Supervision, and SHGs
details: Terms of Credit: Interest rate, collateral security, documentation requirements, and repayment mode/schedule.
Collateral: Borrower assets (land title, bank FD, livestock, house) pledged to lenders as security until full loan clearance.

Formal Credit Sector: Commercial banks & cooperatives regulated by RBI; offers low interest rates (8-12% p.a.), requires formal collateral & documentation. RBI monitors cash reserves and priority sector lending (farmers, small micro-enterprises).
Informal Credit Sector: Moneylenders, traders, landlords, relatives; unregulated, charges exorbitant interest (36-60% p.a.), uses coercive recovery methods, exploits lack of collateral.

Self-Help Groups (SHGs): 15-20 rural members (predominantly women) pooling weekly savings (₹25-100) to grant small internal micro-loans. After 1-2 years of regular savings, SHGs secure collateral-free bank loans.
evidence_or_examples: Megha's housing loan: ₹5 lakh at 12% interest for 10 years backed by salary slips and house title papers pledged as collateral.
Grameen Bank of Bangladesh (founded by Nobel laureate Prof. Muhammad Yunus) proving that poor women are reliable borrowers when organized into peer credit groups.

details: Multinational Corporations (MNCs): Enterprise owning or controlling production facilities in more than one nation.

MNC Location Strategy: Research in developed nations (USA/Europe), manufacturing in low-cost countries (China), assembly & technical customer support in English-speaking nations (India). Reduces production cost by 50-60%.

Interlinking Global Production: (1) Setting up joint ventures with local domestic firms, (2) Acquiring established local companies for immediate market reach, (3) Placing sub-contracting orders with small garment/footwear producers.
evidence_or_examples: American MNC Cargill Foods acquiring Parakh Foods (Indian company with 4 oil refineries and vast distribution network), becoming India's top edible oil producer.
Ford Motors investing ₹1,700 crore near Chennai with Mahindra & Mahindra to manufacture cars for Indian and export markets.

branches.theme: 4.2 Enablers of Globalisation: Technology & Liberalisation Policy

sub_branches.concept: Transportation, IT Revolution, and 1991 Economic Reforms
details: Transportation Advances: Containerization enables fast, low-cost multi-modal freight handling across ports, railways, and trucks.
Information & Communication Technology (ICT): Internet, telecommunications, satellite communication, and digital design allow instantaneous cross-border service exports.
Trade Barriers: Quotas and import tariffs used post-independence (1950s-1980s) to protect infant domestic industries.
1991 Liberalisation Reform: Indian government removed foreign trade & investment barriers, encouraging MNC entry and market competition.
evidence_or_examples: London news magazine designed and typeset in Delhi using satellite text transmission, printed in India, and air-freighted back to London.
Container ships reducing port unloading turn-around time from days to hours while cutting freight costs.

details: World Trade Organisation (WTO): International body establishing rules for free global trade, comprising 164 member nations.
WTO Power Imbalance: Developed countries retain massive domestic agricultural subsidies while pressuring developing nations to dismantle trade barriers.

Uneven Impact in India: Benefited wealthy urban consumers (choice, quality, lower prices), large Indian MNCs (Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy expanding globally), and IT service sector. Severely hurt small manufacturers (capacitors, batteries, plastic toys shutting down) and unorganized laborers facing flexible/insecure jobs.
Fair Globalisation Policy: Government interventions needed to strictly enforce labor laws, provide credit/tech support to small units, and form developing-nation alliances at WTO.
evidence_or_examples: Ravi's capacitor manufacturing unit in Hosur forced to lay off workers and close due to duty-free capacitor imports post-1992.
Special Economic Zones (SEZs) providing 5-year tax holidays, world-class utilities, and flexible labor laws to attract MNC FDI.

branches.theme: 5.1 Marketplace Vulnerability & Evolution of Consumer Movement

sub_branches.concept: Market Power Asymmetry & Grassroots Consumer Activism
details: Marketplace Exploitation: Consumers face adulteration, hoarding, black marketing, false advertising, under-weighing, and unaddressed post-sale defects due to 'caveat emptor' (buyer beware).
Consumer Movement in India: Emerging in the 1960s as a social movement against food shortages, black marketing, and adulteration of edible oil/grains.
Legislative Milestone: Passage of Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) in December 1986 (amended 2019), establishing statutory consumer rights and judicial enforcement.
evidence_or_examples: National Consumers Day celebrated on December 24 annually in India.
Protests in 1970s leading to official publication of consumer price guides and establishment of consumer groups.

branches.theme: 5.2 Six Statutory Consumer Rights & Quality Certification Marks

details: Right to Safety: Protection against life-threatening products and services (e.g. medical negligence, defective electrical appliances).
Right to Information: Mandated disclosure of ingredients, price (MRP), batch number, manufacturing date, and expiry date. Reinforced by Right to Information (RTI) Act 2005 for government operations.
Right to Choose: Freedom to select products without forced conditional bundling by sellers.
Right to be Heard / Representation: Right to file complaints and be represented in consumer forums.
Right to Seek Redressal: Right to receive fair compensation, repair, or replacement for defective goods or deficient services.
Right to Consumer Education: Access to knowledge regarding consumer rights and market awareness.

Quality Certification Logos: Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) seals certifying product safety: ISI Mark (electrical/industrial items), Agmark (agricultural food produce), Hallmark (gold/silver jewelry), FSSAI (processed food safety).
evidence_or_examples: Reji Mathew case: Class IX student paralyzed due to defective hospital anesthesia awarded ₹5 lakh compensation by Consumer Commission under Right to Safety.
Abirami's defective wall clock purchase demonstrating importance of securing a cash receipt/bill as legal evidence for consumer forum claims.

branches.theme: 5.3 Three-Tier Quasi-Judicial Redressal System & Systemic Challenges

details: Three-Tier Quasi-Judicial Hierarchy (COPRA 2019 Rules):
1. District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: Handles claims up to ₹1 crore.
2. State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: Handles claims between ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore, plus appeals against District Commission orders.
3. National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (New Delhi): Handles claims exceeding ₹10 crore, plus appeals against State Commission orders. Final appeal lies with Supreme Court.
Implementation Challenges: Lengthy legal delays, expensive advocate fees, lack of cash receipts/bills from informal shopkeepers, and weak enforcement of court orders.
evidence_or_examples: Consumer filing case in District Commission for a defective ₹25 lakh luxury car, advancing to State Commission if dissatisfied with judgment.
